question: The Italian Government’s ‘Energy Decree’ of 27 November 2023 classified the construction of an onshore regasification plant in Porto Empedocle as an urgent, non-deferrable public interest project. The project was submitted in 2004, receiving a positive Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) in 2008 and being given the go-ahead by the Sicilian Regional Council in 2009.

However, following seizure of the site in 2013 by the Palermo Anti-Mafia District Directorate, the works were never carried out. The 14-kilometre-long Snam pipeline, which would connect the regasification plant to the national network, runs close to the archaeological park of the Valley of the Temples, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In May 2022, Agrigento’s Office for Cultural and Environmental Heritage labelled the project a threat to the site. On 15 September 2023, a regional decree extended the deadline for the completion of the project to 29 April 2028. In view of the above: 1.
Given that the project’s EIA was carried out 16 years ago, does the Commission not believe that a new one is necessary?

Does the Commission not believe that the project runs counter to the Seveso III Directive’s provisions prohibiting the siting of large facilities close to residential areas and cultural heritage sites?
answer: 1. As the Commission stated in its reply to Written Question E-00387/2024, in accordance with Article 8a(6) of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive (1), when deciding to grant development consent the competent authority must be satisfied that any conclusion or decision concluding the EIA process be up-to-date.
Timeframes may be set for the validity of such conclusions or decisions on the environmental impacts of projects.

Where the state of the environment changed after a project was authorised, or new findings regarding the impact of the project on the environment arose between the authorisation of the project and its execution, the assessment may need to be updated accordingly, considering the legitimate expectations of the public and the principle of good administration. 2.

The Seveso III Directive (2) does not prohibit per se the siting of large facilities near residential areas or cultural heritage sites. It sets rules both to prevent major accidents involving dangerous substances and, should such accidents nevertheless occur, to contain any consequences on human health and the environment.

It covers establishments where dangerous substances may be present in quantities exceeding certain thresholds. While a regasification plant could fall within the scope of the directive, pipelines cannot.

Member States must ensure that their policies take into account the directive’s objectives and the need, in the long term, to maintain appropriate safety distances between establishments covered by the directive and residential or recreational areas, buildings and areas of public use, and major transport routes; as well as to protect areas of natural sensitivity or interest near establishments through appropriate measures (3).

Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, p. 1-21, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014, OJ L 124, 25.4.2014, p. 1-18.

Directive 2012/18/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances, amending and subsequently repealing Council Directive 96/82/EC, OJ L 197, 24.7.2012, p. 1-37. Article 13(2) of Directive 2012/18/EU.
